newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori says net reserves $10 billion.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori says net reserves $10 billion.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori said Monday Peru's net international reserves were at $10 billion for the first time in Peru's history.
The reserves stood at $9.996 billion on July 24, according to Peru's Central Reserve Bank.
Fujimori compared the current level of reserves with a negative $200 million reserve level when he took power in 1990.
"Now when Peru has reserves of $10 billion the situation is different," Fujimori told Congress in his annual State of the Nation address.
Peru's reserves have recovered steadily due to tight fiscal policies and a sweeping privatization program since 1990.
Fujimori also said the government had bought back $3.4 billion of the country's debt at a cost of $906 million.

"We have acquired part of the debt that -- including capital and interest -- totalled $3.4 billion at only $906 million," Fujimori said, adding the country's total foreign debt stood at $19.327 billion on June 30.

The president also announced public sector workers would receive a 15 percent pay rise starting in August. The salary increase would mean an additional cost of 500 million soles ($190 million) in the government's budget this year, he added.

Fujimori also said the government's economic policies aimed at increasing exports had resulted in a 20 percent rise in total exports in the first half of the year, compared to the same period last year. He said that, included in this rise, non-traditional exports had increased in the first half by 43 percent.

The government had previously reported that exports grew 16 percent in the first five months of the year to $2.703 billion, compared with the same period last year, according to latest government figures. Non-traditional exports rose 36 percent to $792 million in the first five months of the year.

Fujimori also announced the government would reduce a general housing tax levy from seven to five percent of a worker's salary. Opposition and labor leaders had been calling for the reduction in the tax, whose contributions enter a central government fund for the building of houses and other infrastructure construction.
Fujimori, who is currently mired in political crisis after plummeting recently in the popularity polls, acknowleged "few addresses had been as eagerly awaited" as his speech Monday to Congress.

With most Peruvians calling on Fujimori before the address to draw up a new course for the government to create more jobs and fight poverty, the president said these demands were "totally understandable".
But he said the current political turmoil was an "obvious contradiction" because a "solid economy ... was going hand-in- hand with a confused political situation".
He added: "All our policies have one common denominator -- to create employment and reduce poverty."
Despite Fujimori's conciliatory tone, opposition congressmen, criticized the president for not announcing measures to address the political crisis.

"(The speech) was the same as always," Jorge Avendano opposition legislator for Union for Peru said. "Always (emphasizing) the great economic successes without saying anything to solve the political problem."
